name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3

lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a short peptide linked to a fatty chain, used in some skin-care serums for smoother, firmer-looking skin. It is grouped with the cosmetic signal peptides.

Signal peptides are generally described by manufacturers as messengers that prompt skin cells to repair and rebuild. This specific peptide appears mainly in patent filings that list it among many ingredients, combined with plant extracts and other actives. No human trials of the ingredient on its own were found, and the sources do not describe a tested mechanism for it.

paras: It is applied in leave-on serums and creams, always as one ingredient among several, as part of a daily anti-aging routine.
No safety data specific to this ingredient were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient rather than as an approved drug.

angle.text: Appears in serum ingredient lists as a signal peptide, where users look for smoother, firmer-looking skin. Manufacturers describe signal peptides as prompting skin repair. It is documented in patent formulations with plant extracts.

lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic ingredient classed among the signal peptides, short amino-acid chains attached to a fatty (palmitoyl) group and added to skin-care products so that they dissolve in skin lipids. People use serums and creams containing it for smoother, firmer-looking skin and fewer visible lines. It appears by name in the ingredient lists of published patent compositions for topical products, where it is combined with plant extracts and other actives [1][2][3].

A cosmetic-ingredient database lists palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 as a former name of palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, a peptide with the sequence glycine-glutamine-proline-arginine that is associated with the Matrixyl 3000 complex alongside palmitoyl tripeptide-1; on that page the ingredient is described as reducing interleukin-6 (IL-6) production, which the page links to lower inflammation and slower collagen breakdown [4]. The database cites no studies for these descriptions [4].

No clinical trial of palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 under that name was found, and the available records show it as one listed component of multi-ingredient formulations, so its effect on appearance has not been established by independent human studies.

paras: Signal peptides are short amino-acid chains that manufacturers describe as messengers that prompt skin cells; a palmitic-acid tail is attached to improve oil solubility and skin penetration [4]. Wikipedia describes the better-known palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl) the same way: five amino acids linked to a 16-carbon fatty acid chain that helps the molecule move through skin lipids [5]. Ingredient naming for cosmetic peptides has changed over time; Matrixyl itself was renamed from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 in 2006 [5], and a database page lists palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 as the previous name for palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 [4]. Readers may therefore find tetrapeptide-3 on older labels and patents and tetrapeptide-7 on newer ones.

A family of patent filings from 2008 to 2010 describes compositions containing at least two of a long list of ingredients, among them magnolia extract, honokiol, hesperidin methyl chalcone, gotu kola, a valine-tryptophan dipeptide, ascorbyl glucoside and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 [1][2][3]. These filings illustrate how the peptide is used as one ingredient among many rather than as a stand-alone product.

A related, better-documented cosmetic peptide, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (sold as Matrixyl), was launched by the manufacturer Sederma in 2000 and is promoted for anti-wrinkle use; it is a different molecule from palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 [5].

Matrixyl 3000 is described as combining palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 with palmitoyl tripeptide-1, and is the best-known commercial context for the tetrapeptide [4]. Wikipedia reports that in vitro and in vivo studies, including a 2013 fibroblast collagen study and a 2005 study on photoaged facial skin, have been cited in support of the pentapeptide's anti-wrinkle effect [5].

No studies found under the name palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3. The only records located are patent filings that list the peptide as an ingredient; they do not report human trial results [1][2][3]. Studies of related peptides, such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, have been cited by Wikipedia as supporting anti-wrinkle efficacy but concern a different molecule [5].
No safety data specific to this ingredient were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient rather than as an approved drug.

timeline.event: Sederma launches the related peptide palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 as Matrixyl.[5]
Matrixyl's ingredient name changes from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 to palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.[5]
Patent filings list palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 in magnolia-extract compositions.[1][3]
